grammar.title: Near-synonyms: connotation, collocation and register
grammar.explanation_pt:
No C2, quase-sinônimos raramente são intercambiáveis. Eles se diferenciam em **quatro dimensões**:

**1. Conotação (juízo de valor)**
- positivo → neutro → negativo: **slender** → **thin** → **skinny** → **scrawny**
- **determined** (+) / **persistent** (=) / **stubborn** (−) / **obstinate** (− formal)
- **frugal / thrifty** (+) / **careful with money** (=) / **mean / stingy / tight-fisted** (−)
- **confident** (+) / **self-assured** (=) / **arrogant / cocky** (−)

**2. Collocation (com o que a palavra combina)**
- **commit** a crime / an error ✔ · **make** a mistake ✔ · ❌ commit a mistake
- **heavy** rain / **strong** wind / **high** temperature
- **utterly** combina com palavras negativas ou extremas: utterly **ridiculous / exhausted** (raro: utterly delighted)
- **broad** daylight, **bitterly** cold, **acutely** aware, **painfully** shy, **blissfully** unaware

**3. Registro**
- **commence** (formal) / **start** (neutro) / **kick off** (informal)
- **deceased** (formal/jurídico) / **dead** (neutro) / **passed away** (eufemismo)
- **inebriated** (formal/humorístico) / **drunk** (neutro) / **hammered** (gíria)

**4. Intensidade**
- **like** < **be fond of** < **adore** < **worship**
- **annoyed** < **irritated** < **angry** < **furious** < **livid**
- **interesting** < **fascinating** < **riveting**

**Uso estratégico:** a escolha de palavras revela **posição**. Jornalistas, políticos e advogados escolhem com cuidado: "**reform**" (+) x "**cuts**" (−); "**protesters**" x "**rioters**"; "**estate tax**" x "**death tax**".

examples.en: What her supporters call principled, her critics call obstinate.
examples.pt: O que seus apoiadores chamam de íntegro, seus críticos chamam de obstinado.

examples.en: He was blissfully unaware that the whole office had been talking about him.
examples.pt: Ele estava felizmente alheio ao fato de que o escritório inteiro andava falando dele.

examples.en: The government described the measures as "reforms"; the unions called them "cuts".
examples.pt: O governo descreveu as medidas como "reformas"; os sindicatos as chamaram de "cortes".

grammar.tip_pt: Use um **dicionário de collocations** (como o *Oxford Collocations Dictionary*) e um **corpus** (buscadores de frases reais) para checar combinações. No C2, a pergunta não é "essa palavra existe?", mas "**um nativo diria assim?**"

common_mistakes.why_pt: skinny tem conotação negativa; slender combina com elegância.

common_mistakes.right: He made a mistake. / He committed an error (formal).
common_mistakes.why_pt: commit combina com crime, error, offence — não com mistake.

common_mistakes.right: I was thoroughly / immensely pleased with the result.
common_mistakes.why_pt: utterly costuma combinar com palavras negativas ou absolutas.

pronunciation.tip_pt: A conotação também está no **tom**. A mesma palavra neutra pode ficar negativa com ênfase e entonação: "He's very... *confident*" (com pausa e tom descendente = arrogante). No C2, perceba e use essa camada.

listening.title: Same facts, different words
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de linguística mostra como a escolha de palavras muda a percepção de um mesmo fato.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: In a classic experiment published in 1974, the psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed participants films of car accidents and then asked them how fast the cars were going. The only difference between the groups was a single verb. Some were asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" each other; others heard "collided", "bumped", "hit" or "contacted". Those who heard "smashed" gave the highest speed estimates. A week later, they were also more likely to report having seen broken glass — even though there was none in the film. One word changed not just how people judged the event, but what they remembered. Journalists, lawyers and politicians understand this intuitively. Is a sudden rise in prices a "spike" or a "correction"? Are people who cross a border "migrants", "refugees" or "illegals"? Each choice is a small argument in disguise. And at the highest level of language, noticing those choices — and making them consciously — is perhaps the most important skill of all.

questions.answer: The verb used in the question (smashed, collided, bumped, hit, contacted).

questions.q: What happened a week later?
questions.answer: The "smashed" group were more likely to report seeing broken glass, though there was none.

questions.q: What does the speaker mean by "a small argument in disguise"?
questions.answer: Word choice subtly expresses a position or judgement.

reading.title: The tyranny of the thesaurus
reading.text: Every writing teacher has encountered it: the essay in which every second word appears to have been lifted from a thesaurus. "The protagonist perambulated pensively through the verdant arboretum", writes the student, when what he means is that the main character walked through the park, thinking. The impulse is understandable. Learners — and, for that matter, many native speakers — are often taught that variety is a virtue and that repetition is a sin. A thesaurus seems to offer an endless supply of alternatives. The difficulty is that a thesaurus lists words that are similar, not words that are interchangeable. "Slender", "skinny", "gaunt" and "emaciated" all denote thinness, but they evoke four very different people. "Notorious" and "famous" both describe someone widely known, yet only one would be welcome on a reference letter. Even apparently neutral synonyms differ in collocation and register: one "commences" a legal procedure but rarely "commences" a holiday. Linguists sometimes claim that there are no true synonyms in any language — that if two words were genuinely identical in every context, one of them would eventually fall out of use or acquire a distinct meaning. Whether or not this is strictly true, it captures something important. Words carry histories, associations and social signals that no list can fully record. The solution is not to abandon the thesaurus but to treat it as a starting point rather than an answer. Before adopting an unfamiliar word, a careful writer checks how it is actually used: in which contexts, with which neighbours, in what tone. Precision, not variety, is the hallmark of good writing — and, at the highest levels of proficiency, of good speaking too. As the novelist Elmore Leonard memorably advised: if it sounds like writing, rewrite it.

questions.q: What is the problem with the student's sentence?
questions.answer: It uses unnecessarily elaborate thesaurus words instead of simple, natural ones.

questions.q: What does a thesaurus list, according to the text?
questions.answer: Words that are similar, not interchangeable.

questions.q: What do some linguists claim about synonyms?
questions.answer: That there are no true synonyms; identical words would fall out of use or change meaning.

questions.q: What is the hallmark of good writing, according to the writer?
questions.answer: Precision, not variety.

writing.model:
Reference for Mr. André Santos

To whom it may concern,

I am pleased to provide a reference for André Santos, who worked as a Senior Analyst in my team at Horizonte Consultoria from March 2021 to June 2025.

André is a highly capable analyst with an exceptional eye for detail. His reports were consistently thorough and meticulously researched, and on several occasions he identified errors in financial models that others had overlooked. Clients frequently commented on the clarity of his written work.

He is also a determined professional. When a project encountered difficulties, he was invariably the last person to give up, and he often worked well beyond what was expected of him to meet a deadline. This persistence was particularly valuable during a complex restructuring project in 2023, which he helped to bring to a successful conclusion.

André holds strong views on how work should be done and expresses them directly. While this occasionally led to lively discussions within the team, his contributions were always motivated by a genuine commitment to quality. He would, I believe, thrive in a role that allows him a degree of independence and values precision above speed.

I have no hesitation in recommending him for a position that requires analytical rigour and dedication. Should you require any further information, please do not hesitate to contact me.

Yours faithfully,

Mariana Duarte
Head of Analysis, Horizonte Consultoria

—
Word choices: "determined" rather than "stubborn" emphasizes the positive side of his persistence; "expresses them directly" is a neutral way of acknowledging that he could be blunt; "lively discussions" signals conflict without exaggerating it.

warmup.text_pt: "Ela **não é nada boba**" significa que ela é esperta. "**Não foi pouca coisa**" significa que foi uma grande conquista. No C2, você também precisa dominar as **negações enfáticas**: "by no means", "far from", "anything but".

grammar.title: Emphatic negation and litotes
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Negação enfática** — reforça o "não":
- **by no means / not by any means** (de modo algum): "The result is **by no means** certain."
- **not in the least / not in the slightest / not at all**: "I'm **not in the least** worried."
- **far from** + adjetivo/-ing/substantivo (longe de): "The plan is **far from** perfect." / "**Far from** helping, he made things worse."
- **anything but** (tudo menos): "The meeting was **anything but** productive."
- **nowhere near** (nem perto de): "We're **nowhere near** ready."
- **not remotely / not the least bit**: "It's **not remotely** funny."
- No início da frase → **inversão**: "**By no means** is this the end." / "**In no way** am I criticizing you."

**2. None too / none the + comparativo**
- **none too** + adjetivo (= not very, irônico): "He was **none too** happy about it."
- **none the** + comparativo (= not at all + comparativo): "I read the instructions twice and was **none the wiser**." (não entendi nada mais) / "He fell but was **none the worse for** it." (não sofreu nada)

**3. Litotes** — afirmar algo negando o oposto (understatement elegante):
- **not bad** (= bom) · **not uncommon** (= bastante comum) · **not unlike** (= parecido com) · **not without** (= com algum) · **no small** / **no mean** (= grande)
- "It was **no mean feat**." / "The idea is **not without** its problems." / "His style is **not unlike** Hemingway's."
- Efeito: soa **cauteloso, irônico ou modesto**.

**4. Not so much X as Y** (não tanto X, mas sim Y):
- "It's **not so much** a problem **as** an opportunity."

**5. Implicatura** — o que se comunica sem dizer:
- "Some of the students passed." → implica que **nem todos** passaram.
- "Can you pass the salt?" → não é uma pergunta sobre habilidade.
- "He's a good typist." (numa carta de referência para professor universitário) → implica que **não há nada mais** a elogiar.

listening.title: What we mean when we don't say it
listening.context_pt: Um filósofo da linguagem explica as máximas de Grice num podcast.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: In the 1960s and 1970s, the British philosopher Paul Grice proposed that conversation is guided by what he called the Cooperative Principle. We assume that the people we talk to are trying to communicate efficiently, and he described several "maxims" they generally follow: say as much as is needed but no more; say what you believe to be true; be relevant; and be clear. The fascinating part is what happens when someone appears to break a maxim. Suppose I ask a friend, "How was the restaurant?" and she replies, "Well, the parking was easy." She's apparently being irrelevant. But because I assume she's cooperating, I infer something she hasn't said: the food was by no means good. Grice called this kind of meaning an "implicature". It's how irony works, how politeness works, and how a great deal of everyday communication works. And it's often where advanced learners struggle — not with the words, but with what lies between them.

questions.q: What is the Cooperative Principle?
questions.answer: The assumption that people in conversation are trying to communicate efficiently.

questions.q: Name two of Grice's maxims.

questions.q: What does the friend imply by "the parking was easy"?
questions.answer: That the food was not good.

questions.q: Where do advanced learners often struggle, according to the speaker?

reading.title: The art of saying less
reading.text: English, and British English in particular, has a reputation for understatement, and few devices capture this more neatly than litotes: the practice of asserting something by denying its opposite. To describe a brilliant performance as "not bad", a catastrophic error as "not ideal" or a significant achievement as "no mean feat" is to communicate, paradoxically, by appearing to say less than one means. The device is far from new. It appears in Old English poetry, where a hero might be said to be "not unfamiliar" with battle, and it was a favourite of classical rhetoricians, who valued it as a way of sounding modest while making a strong point. Why should speakers choose such an indirect route? Part of the answer lies in social risk. Unrestrained praise can sound insincere; unrestrained criticism can sound aggressive. Litotes offers a way of expressing judgement while leaving room for retreat. A manager who calls a report "not without its problems" can, if challenged, insist that she meant only minor issues — even if both parties know she meant something rather more serious. There is also an aesthetic dimension. Understatement invites the listener to participate, to reconstruct the full meaning from the restrained version. When it works, it creates a sense of shared understanding, almost of complicity. Yet the same quality makes litotes treacherous for anyone unfamiliar with the code. A visitor who takes "not bad" at face value may underestimate genuine enthusiasm, while one who takes "it's not the worst idea I've heard" as encouragement may be in for a disappointment. At the highest levels of proficiency, then, understanding English is by no means simply a matter of knowing words. It is a matter of knowing how much — and how little — they are being asked to carry.

grammar.title: Binomials, proverbs and creative manipulation
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Binômios (binomials)** — pares de palavras ligados por **and / or / but**, com **ordem fixa**:
- **Sinônimos/reforço:** safe and sound, peace and quiet, pick and choose, first and foremost
- **Opostos:** pros and cons, ups and downs, give and take, sooner or later, black and white, back and forth
- **Repetição/rima:** neck and neck (empatados), touch and go, wear and tear, high and dry, rough and ready
- **Preposições:** by and large, on and off, over and above, out and about
⚠️ A ordem **não muda**: ❌ "sound and safe", ❌ "cons and pros".

**Trinômios:** lock, stock and barrel (tudo); hook, line and sinker (completamente); tall, dark and handsome.

**2. Provérbios** — nativos frequentemente dizem **só a primeira metade**:
- "When in Rome..." (do as the Romans do)
- "Speak of the devil..." (and he shall appear) — quando alguém de quem se falava aparece
- "Too many cooks..." (spoil the broth)
- "The early bird..." (catches the worm)
- "Every cloud..." (has a silver lining)
- "Don't count your chickens..." (before they hatch)

**3. Manipulação criativa** — manchetes, publicidade e humor alteram expressões fixas, e o leitor C2 precisa reconhecer o original:
- "**Every cloud has a silver lining**" → manchete sobre computação em nuvem: "**Every cloud has a cyber lining**"
- "**Better late than never**" → "**Better late than pregnant**" (humor)
- "**All's well that ends well**" → "All's well that **sends** well" (anúncio de correio)

**4. Uso adequado** — idioms em excesso soam **artificiais** ("It's raining cats and dogs, so let's kill two birds with one stone..."). Use-os **com moderação** e no **registro certo**: "by and large" e "first and foremost" funcionam até em textos formais; "lock, stock and barrel" é mais informal/jornalístico.

listening.title: Why can't we say "pepper and salt"?
listening.context_pt: Uma linguista explica por que binômios têm ordem fixa.

lines.speaker: Linguist
lines.en: Why do English speakers say "salt and pepper" but never "pepper and salt"? Or "rock and roll", "black and white", "ladies and gentlemen"? Linguists have identified several tendencies — not strict rules, but strong patterns. First, the shorter word tends to come first: "salt and pepper", "bread and butter". Second, when vowels differ, words with higher, front vowels — like the "i" in "zig" — tend to precede lower, back vowels, like the "a" in "zag". That's why it's "zig-zag", "tick-tock", "flip-flop" and never the other way round. Third, cultural or logical priority often matters: "cause and effect", "before and after", "husband and wife" — though the last example also shows how these orders can reflect social hierarchies of the past. Interestingly, Portuguese often shows similar patterns. But when the orders differ between languages, learners tend to transfer their own — which is why, at C2, these small, fixed pairs are worth learning as single units.

questions.q: Which word tends to come first in a binomial?
questions.answer: The shorter word.

questions.q: What vowel pattern explains "zig-zag" and "tick-tock"?

reading.title: The headline writer's toolkit
reading.text: Few writers handle fixed expressions with as much mischief as the authors of newspaper headlines. Limited to a handful of words and competing for the reader's attention, headline writers — sub-editors, in British newsrooms — have long relied on a simple trick: take a familiar phrase and twist it. A story about a theft from a cheese factory becomes "Grate Expectations"; an article on the decline of hand-written letters is headed "Signed, Sealed, Deleted"; a report on rising house prices in a seaside town appears as "Home and Dry? Not Any More". The technique depends entirely on recognition. The reader must instantly recall the original — Dickens's Great Expectations, the song "Signed, Sealed, Delivered", the idiom "home and dry" — and register the change. The pleasure lies in the gap between the expected and the actual, and in the small flash of understanding that bridges it. Advertising uses the same mechanism, as do comedians, politicians and, increasingly, social media users. For language learners, this presents a particular challenge. It is perfectly possible to understand every word of a headline and still miss its point entirely. A learner unfamiliar with "Every cloud has a silver lining" will find nothing remarkable in a technology column titled "Every Cloud Has a Cyber Lining"; the native reader, by contrast, sees a joke, an argument and a cultural reference compressed into six words. This is why fixed expressions matter far more at the highest levels than their apparent triviality might suggest. They are part and parcel of a shared cultural memory — the background against which a great deal of creative language is written. To read like an insider, one must first know what the insiders know by heart. Only then can one appreciate, and eventually produce, the twist.

questions.q: What does the technique depend on?

questions.q: Why can learners miss the point of a headline?

Home Sweet Office

When my company announced that we would be working from home "for the foreseeable future", I was, first and foremost, delighted. No more traffic, no more crowded lifts, no more colleagues reheating fish in the office microwave. Peace and quiet at last.

That was three years ago. By and large, I don't regret it. But I have learned that working from home has its ups and downs, and that some of them are not entirely obvious at first.

Take the kitchen table. In theory, it's a temporary workspace. In practice, it has become my office lock, stock and barrel: laptop, second screen, a mountain of papers and an assortment of odds and ends that I'm afraid to throw away. My family now eats dinner on the sofa.

Then there are the interruptions. Unexpected deliveries, the neighbour's renovations and a cat who believes my keyboard is a heated bed are, it seems, part and parcel of the arrangement. Last month, during an important video call with a client, it was touch and go whether I would finish my presentation before the drilling next door began. (It began.)

The biggest surprise, however, has been loneliness. Real conversations with colleagues are now few and far between. I never imagined I would miss Paulo from accounts and his endless stories about his weekend fishing trips. But I do.

So, after weighing up the pros and cons, I've reached a compromise. Twice a week, I go to a co-working space. It's rough and ready — the coffee is terrible — but there are people, and conversation, and nobody is drilling.

Is working from home the be-all and end-all? Not quite. But sooner or later, I suspect, most of us will find our own balance. Meanwhile, the cat has the keyboard.

grammar.title: Absolute constructions
grammar.explanation_pt:
Uma **oração absoluta** tem **sujeito próprio** (diferente do da oração principal) e um particípio, adjetivo, advérbio ou locução — **sem verbo conjugado**. Ela acrescenta circunstância (tempo, causa, condição, descrição).

**1. Substantivo + particípio (-ing / -ed)**
- "**The work done**, we went home." (= When the work was done...)
- "**The sun having set**, the temperature dropped."
- "**Weather permitting**, the ceremony will be held outdoors."
- "**Other things being equal**, the cheaper option is better."

**2. Substantivo + adjetivo / advérbio / locução** (muito comum em descrições literárias):
- "**The meeting over**, they left."
- "She stood at the window, **her face pale**."
- "He walked in, **hands in his pockets**."
- "The children ran out, **their schoolbags forgotten**."

**3. With / Without + objeto + particípio/adjetivo/locução** (mais natural na fala):
- "**With prices rising**, families are cutting back."
- "**With the deadline approaching**, nobody slept."
- "She fell asleep **with the light on**."
- "**Without anyone noticing**, he slipped out."

**4. Expressões absolutas fixas** (sem sujeito explícito, aceitas como "comentário"):
- **generally / strictly / broadly / frankly speaking** · **all things considered** · **considering** + noun · **given** + noun · **judging by / from** · **assuming** · **that said / that being said** · **talking of** · **taking everything into account**

**5. Cuidado com o dangling participle** (erro de sujeito):
- ❌ "**Walking** to the station, **the rain** started." (a chuva estava andando?)
- ✅ "**Walking** to the station, **I** got caught in the rain." (mesmo sujeito)
- ✅ "**I was walking** to the station **when** the rain started."
- As **expressões fixas** do item 4 são exceções aceitas.

listening.title: Travel writing at its best
listening.context_pt: Um editor de literatura de viagem fala sobre o que torna um relato memorável.

lines.speaker: Editor
lines.en: What separates great travel writing from a guidebook? Generally speaking, it's the shift from information to experience. A guidebook tells you the museum opens at nine. A travel writer puts you on the steps outside at ten to nine, the street still wet from the night's rain, a stray dog asleep in a patch of sunlight. Notice the grammar there — those little phrases with their own subjects, "the street still wet", "a dog asleep". They let a writer add layers of detail without stopping the flow of the sentence. Writers like Jan Morris, Bruce Chatwin and Paul Theroux used them constantly. The other ingredient is honesty. The best travel writers aren't afraid to describe disappointment, boredom or their own prejudices — and, all things considered, that's what makes us trust them when they describe wonder.

reading.title: Dawn in Ouro Preto
reading.text: I arrived in Ouro Preto after midnight, the bus from Belo Horizonte having been delayed by fog on the mountain road, and I remember almost nothing of that first night except the cold and the sound of rain on a tiled roof. It was the morning that stayed with me. I woke before six, the room still dark, and, unable to sleep, went out to walk. The town, built on hills so steep that some streets seem to defy gravity, was entirely silent. Mist lay in the valleys between the churches, their towers rising out of it like the masts of ships at anchor. The cobblestones, polished by three centuries of feet and that night's rain, shone under the last of the streetlamps. Somewhere below, a dog barked once, then thought better of it. I climbed towards the Church of São Francisco de Assis, my breath visible in the air, my legs protesting at every step. With the light growing stronger, details began to emerge: the soapstone carvings above the doorway, the blue and white of colonial façades, a woman in a doorway sweeping her front step, her radio murmuring a morning programme. She nodded to me without a word, as if strangers at dawn were part and parcel of her day. History in Ouro Preto is not a subject but an atmosphere. Gold made the town rich in the eighteenth century, its wealth flowing to Lisbon and beyond, and the beauty that remains was built, in large part, by enslaved labour — a fact no honest visitor should forget. Yet that morning, the streets empty and the mist slowly lifting, it felt less like a museum than a place still dreaming. By eight, the first tour buses had arrived. The spell broken, I went in search of coffee. All things considered, I have rarely spent two hours better.

writing.model:
Saturday at the Ver-o-Peso

I arrived at the Ver-o-Peso market in Belém just after five, the sky over the Guajará Bay still the colour of slate. The boats had come in during the night, their decks piled high with baskets of açaí, and men were already carrying them ashore, the purple fruit glistening in the half-light.

The noise came first. Vendors shouted prices to one another across the stalls, a radio somewhere played brega at full volume, and the vultures — there are always vultures at the Ver-o-Peso — circled above the fish market with an air of patient expectation. Then came the smells: river mud, diesel, coriander, the sharp, sweet scent of cupuaçu.

I wandered through the herb section, where women sat behind tables crowded with bottles and roots, each labelled with promises. One mixture, I was told, would bring luck in love; another, prosperity in business; a third, a combination of both. The seller, a woman in her seventies, her hair tied back in a bright scarf, explained each one with the seriousness of a pharmacist. When I asked whether they really worked, she smiled and said nothing, which seemed the most honest answer possible.

By seven, the heat had arrived. With the sun climbing higher and the crowds growing thicker, I retreated to a stall by the water for breakfast: fried fish, farinha and a bowl of açaí so thick that the spoon stood upright in it. Around me, porters sat in silence, their work done for the morning, staring out at the river.

The market will doubtless change. There are always plans to modernize, to clean up, to make it more "tourist-friendly". Some of those changes may be welcome. But that morning, the river shining and the vultures still circling, it felt like the beating heart of the city — chaotic, generous and entirely alive.

All things considered, I can think of few better places to understand the Amazon without leaving the city.
